title: The Bishop of Digne
text: In 1815 the little town of Digne, in the mountains of the south of France, has had for nine years a bishop unlike any other. Monseigneur Myriel is seventy-five, and the poor call him Monseigneur Bienvenu, “Welcome.” Three days after arriving he gave his palace to the hospital and moved into its cramped house; he gives away nearly all his income, tours his diocese on foot or on a donkey, and once crossed bandit country alone to reach a village of shepherds. He lives with his gentle sister, Mademoiselle Baptistine, and their bustling servant, Madame Magloire, who have both learned to live by his fearless ways.

Hugo spends these chapters showing what the Bishop is rather than telling a story about him: his mild wit, his indulgence toward the weak, the day he spent beside a condemned man on the scaffold, and his visit to a dying old revolutionary shunned by the whole town, which ends with the Bishop on his knees asking the old man’s blessing. His one fault, the narrator says, was a royalist coldness toward Napoleon in his fall.
As chapter 14 closes, nothing has yet happened to this good man. He keeps only two luxuries, six silver forks and spoons and a pair of silver candlesticks, and his front door has no lock.

title: The convict and the candlesticks
text: In Digne in 1815 lives Monseigneur Myriel, a saintly old bishop whom the poor call Bienvenu, “Welcome.” He has given his palace to the sick and his income to the poor, and he never locks his door. His only luxuries are some silver tableware and two silver candlesticks.

One October evening a ragged, exhausted traveller is turned away from every inn and door in town, even a dog’s kennel. At the Bishop’s house he announces the worst at once: he is Jean Valjean, a convict just released after nineteen years in the galleys of Toulon, carrying the yellow passport that marks him everywhere. The Bishop sets another place with the silver and gives him a bed. Hugo then tells his story. A tree-pruner who stole a loaf for his sister’s seven starving children, he got five years and, after four escape attempts, served nineteen, and the galleys turned him into a man who hates society and God.

In the night Valjean steals the silver and flees over the garden wall. When gendarmes drag him back, the Bishop says he gave it to him, hands him the candlesticks as well, and tells him that he has bought his soul for God and that he has promised to use the silver to become an honest man.

Valjean wanders the fields in turmoil and, almost without thinking, puts his foot on a coin dropped by a little Savoyard chimney-sweep, Petit-Gervais, and drives the boy away. Then, horrified at himself, he searches in vain for the child and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. As chapter 27 closes, a man has been seen that night kneeling in prayer at the Bishop’s door, and Valjean is changed, though the narrator does not yet say into what.

title: Fantine’s summer
text: In Digne in 1815 the saintly Bishop Myriel took in Jean Valjean, a convict released after nineteen years in the galleys for stealing a loaf. Valjean robbed him of his silver in the night; when the gendarmes brought him back, the Bishop said it was a gift, added his two silver candlesticks, and told him he had bought his soul for God. Shaken, Valjean then robbed a little chimney-sweep, Petit-Gervais, of a coin, and wept with remorse when the boy was gone.

Hugo leaves him there and jumps to Paris in 1817. Four students, led by the rich, witty Félix Tholomyès, spend a bright summer Sunday at Saint-Cloud with their four young working-girl mistresses. Among the girls is Fantine, a foundling from Montreuil-sur-Mer, beautiful and modest, for whom Tholomyès is a first and only love. All day the men promise the girls a “surprise.”

After dinner at Bombarda’s the men kiss the girls and slip out. The surprise is a letter: they have taken the coach home to their families and respectability, and the affair is over. The other girls laugh it off. As chapter 36 closes, Fantine laughs too, then weeps alone, for she has a little child by Tholomyès.

title: The Lark of Montfermeil
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne answered the theft of his silver by the released convict Jean Valjean with a gift of his candlesticks, telling him he had bought his soul for God. Valjean, after robbing a little chimney-sweep of a coin, wept with remorse; the narrator has said no more of him since.

In Paris in 1817 Fantine, a young working girl, was abandoned by her lover, the student Tholomyès, who went home to his family and left her with their small daughter, Cosette. Ten months later, with no money and no work, she walks out of Paris toward her native town of Montreuil-sur-Mer. At Montfermeil she passes an inn where two happy little girls are swinging, and she leaves Cosette with their mother, Madame Thénardier, paying in advance and promising monthly payments.

The Thénardiers are a nasty pair: she is a coarse brute who loves only her own daughters, Éponine and Azelma; he is a scheming innkeeper who boasts of having been a sergeant at Waterloo. They pawn Cosette’s clothes, dress her in rags, feed her under the table with the dog and cat, and keep inventing reasons to raise the price. As chapter 39 closes, Cosette is about five, the household drudge, beaten by Madame Thénardier and scorned by the girls, and the village calls her the Lark. Her mother, far away, keeps paying.

title: The mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne forgave the released convict Jean Valjean for stealing his silver and gave him the candlesticks too; Valjean, after robbing a little chimney-sweep, wept with remorse and vanished from the story. In 1817 the young Fantine was abandoned in Paris by her lover Tholomyès and left their daughter, Cosette, with the Thénardiers, innkeepers at Montfermeil, who make the child their drudge and keep raising what they charge her mother.

Fantine has gone home to Montreuil-sur-Mer and found it transformed. In December 1815 a stranger arrived with a knapsack and a stick, saved two children from a fire, and revolutionised the local trade in black glass trinkets. Father Madeleine, as everyone calls him, has built a great factory that employs anyone willing to be honest, poured his profits into schools and hospital beds, and in 1820 was made mayor. He is quiet, solitary and enormously strong; when the papers report the death of the Bishop of Digne, he goes into mourning and says he served in the family in his youth. Only one man distrusts him: Javert, a police inspector born in a prison, who worships authority and despises anyone who has ever broken the law. When old Fauchelevent, a carter who dislikes the mayor, is pinned under his cart, Javert remarks that he has known only one man strong enough to lift it, a convict at Toulon. Madeleine crawls under and lifts it, then finds Fauchelevent a post as gardener at a convent in Paris.

Fantine worked in the mayor’s factory until a gossip discovered her child and the forewoman dismissed her in his name, without his knowing. Lying letters from the Thénardiers drove her to sell her hair, then her front teeth, then herself. Hating the mayor she blames for her ruin, she becomes a prostitute.

One snowy night a dandy named Bamatabois stuffs snow down her back; she claws him, and Javert sentences her to six months in prison. Madeleine walks in, orders her released, and, when she spits in his face, overrules the furious Javert and promises her that her debts would be paid and her child brought to her. As chapter 52 closes, Fantine has fainted kissing his hand, and Javert has been humiliated in front of a prostitute.

title: The Champmathieu affair
text: In 1815 the Bishop of Digne forgave the released convict Jean Valjean for stealing his silver, gave him his candlesticks too, and told him he had bought his soul for God; Valjean robbed a little Savoyard, Petit-Gervais, of a coin, then wept with remorse. In 1817 Fantine, abandoned by her lover, left her daughter Cosette with the Thénardiers at Montfermeil, who mistreat the child and bleed her mother for money. At Montreuil-sur-Mer the good mayor, Father Madeleine, rescued Fantine, ruined and sick, from Inspector Javert.

Madeleine nurses Fantine and sends the Thénardiers money to bring Cosette, but Thénardier, smelling profit, invents bills and keeps the child, and Fantine is dying of a chest disease. Then Javert comes to ask to be dismissed. In his anger he denounced the mayor to Paris as the escaped convict Jean Valjean, and he was wrong: the real Jean Valjean has been found, an old apple-thief called Champmathieu whom three former convicts have recognised. He goes on trial at Arras tomorrow and faces the galleys for life.

Now the narrator says plainly what the reader may have guessed: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean. Through a night of torment he argues both ways, to stay silent and go on doing good for a whole town and for Fantine and her child, or to give himself up and keep his soul. He burns his convict’s clothes and the coin he took from Petit-Gervais, and drives to Arras through a chain of breakdowns that seem to beg him to turn back.

In the courtroom he sees a bewildered old man who looks like himself as he entered Digne, condemned by everyone’s certainty. He stands up, tells the court that he is Jean Valjean, proves it with details only the three convicts could know, and walks out with no one daring to stop him. As chapter 65 closes, Champmathieu has been freed, and the mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer has named himself a convict before the whole court, while Fantine still waits for her child.

title: Fantine dies, Valjean flees
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy in 1815, remade himself as M. Madeleine, the beloved manufacturer and mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer. He took in Fantine, a ruined, dying young mother whose daughter, Cosette, is a drudge at the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil, and promised to bring her the child. Then, to save an innocent old man, Champmathieu, from the galleys in his place, he declared himself Jean Valjean in open court at Arras.

He comes back at dawn with his hair turned white and goes straight to Fantine, whose first word is “Cosette?” Then Javert appears in the doorway with a warrant, seizes him by the collar, and shouts that there is no mayor, only the convict Jean Valjean. Fantine, learning that her child was never brought, dies of the shock. Valjean lays out her body, whispers something in her ear, and gives himself up.

That night he breaks out of the town jail, slips back to his room, wraps up the Bishop’s candlesticks and leaves money for the poor. When Javert bursts in, Sister Simplice, the nun who has never told a lie, tells him two and saves Valjean. The town turns against its former mayor the moment it hears he was a convict, and Fantine is buried in a common grave.
As chapter 70 closes, Valjean has vanished toward Paris with Javert on his trail, and Cosette is still at Montfermeil, her mother dead and the man who meant to fetch her a hunted fugitive.

title: The field of Waterloo
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, the good mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, until he gave himself up in court to save an innocent man who had been taken for him. Inspector Javert arrested him at the bedside of Fantine, the ruined young mother he had promised to reunite with her daughter, and she died of the shock. Valjean broke out of jail and fled toward Paris. Cosette, Fantine’s child, remains a drudge at the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil.

Volume II opens with a long detour. In 1861 the narrator walks onto the battlefield of Waterloo and retells the battle of 18 June 1815: the rain that delayed Napoleon’s guns, the hidden hollow road of Ohain that swallowed the French cuirassiers, the late arrival of the Prussians, the death of the Imperial Guard, and Cambronne’s defiant word. Hugo reads the day as chance and Providence rather than genius, and Waterloo as the victory of the old monarchies over the Revolution, ushering in the Restoration of the Bourbons.

Then he returns to the field by moonlight, where marauders strip the dead. One prowler, with a sutler’s cart nearby, robs a buried cavalry officer of his ring, cross, watch and purse, and in doing so drags him alive from under the corpses in the hollow road. The officer, believing himself rescued, asks his name: Thénardier. His own is Pontmercy. As chapter 89 closes, the reader knows what kind of “sergeant at Waterloo” the Montfermeil innkeeper was, and an officer named Pontmercy believes he owes him his life.

title: Convict number 9,430
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, the good mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, until he gave himself up in court to save an innocent man taken for him. Javert arrested him at the bedside of Fantine, the ruined mother he had promised to reunite with her daughter, and she died of the shock; Valjean broke out of jail and fled toward Paris. Cosette is still a drudge at the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil. And on the night after Waterloo, the narrator has shown, Thénardier was a marauder robbing the dead, and the officer he robbed, Pontmercy, believes Thénardier saved his life.

Two newspaper extracts of July 1823 report that Jean Valjean was recaptured in Paris, tried for the old robbery of Petit-Gervais, condemned to death and reprieved to the galleys for life, and returned to Toulon as convict number 9,430. A large sum he withdrew from the bank of Laffitte before his arrest has never been found. Without him, Montreuil-sur-Mer’s prosperity collapses. Near Montfermeil an ex-convict road-mender, Boulatruelle, has taken to digging in the forest: he once saw a man he knew from the galleys carry a small chest into the woods and come out with only a pick and shovel.

In late October 1823 the warship Orion, under repair at Toulon, has a sailor left dangling from a yard. A white-haired life convict breaks his ankle chain with a single blow, climbs the rigging and saves him, then falls into the sea between two ships. As chapter 92 closes, the Toulon paper has reported the drowning of convict 9,430, Jean Valjean; his body has not been found.

title: Christmas Eve at Montfermeil
text: Jean Valjean, a convict saved by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, became M. Madeleine, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, and promised the dying Fantine to bring her daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers’ inn at Montfermeil. Then he gave himself up to save an innocent man, Fantine died, and he was retaken and sent back to the galleys at Toulon, where in 1823 he was reported drowned after saving a sailor from the rigging of the Orion.

On Christmas Eve 1823 Cosette, eight years old, bruised and in rags, is sent out alone in the dark with a bucket bigger than she is to fetch water from the forest spring. On the way she stops, spellbound, before a magnificent doll in a toy stall. At the spring, terrified, she struggles back with the bucket until a huge hand silently takes it from her: a white-haired stranger in a shabby yellow coat, who earlier that evening had checked a particular clearing in the forest, is walking beside her, and she is not afraid.

At the inn the Thénardiers take him for a beggar. He watches Cosette, saves her from a beating, buys her the doll from the stall, and slips a gold coin into her wooden shoe on the hearth. In the morning he pays Thénardier’s padded bill and fifteen hundred francs more and walks away with the child. When Thénardier runs after them for more money, the stranger shows a note signed by Fantine telling him to hand Cosette over to the bearer, and a look sends the innkeeper home.

Then the narrator says it outright: Jean Valjean was not dead. He swam from the Orion, made his way to Paris, read that he was believed drowned, and came to Montfermeil to keep his word to Fantine. As chapter 103 closes he is carrying Cosette, asleep with her doll, into Paris toward the Boulevard de l’Hôpital.

title: The Gorbeau house
text: Jean Valjean, the convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy and who became M. Madeleine, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, gave himself up to save an innocent man, was sent back to the galleys, and escaped by letting the world believe he had drowned at Toulon. On Christmas Eve 1823 he kept the promise he had made to the dying Fantine: he took her daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers, who had made the eight-year-old their drudge, and paid them to let her go.

He brings her to an attic in the Gorbeau house, a ramshackle building at the bleak southern edge of Paris. There, for the first time in his life, he loves someone, and Cosette, who has never been loved, loves him back. They live quietly and happily; he teaches her to read and lets her play.

But he goes out only after dark, becomes known in the quarter as “the beggar who gives alms,” and the nosy old woman who keeps the house spies on him and sees him take a thousand-franc note from the lining of his coat. Then he thinks he glimpses Javert’s face under a beggar’s rags. A tall new lodger listens at his door by night, and at dawn Valjean recognises his back. As chapter 108 closes, he has gathered his money and slipped out of the Gorbeau house with Cosette at nightfall.

title: Over the wall
text: Jean Valjean, the convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, then gave himself up to save an innocent man, was sent back to the galleys, and escaped by letting the world believe he had drowned. He took Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers on Christmas Eve 1823 and lived with her happily in the Gorbeau house in Paris, until he realised that Javert had found him and fled with her at nightfall.

Through the moonlit maze of old Paris he sees four men on his trail with Javert at their head. Across the Pont d’Austerlitz and into the empty Petit-Picpus quarter, he is trapped between a blind alley and a sentinel. He cuts down a street lantern’s rope, climbs a high wall by sheer strength, hauls Cosette up after him, and drops with her into a vast, silent garden as the patrol searches the street outside.

The place is strange: barred, dark buildings, women’s voices singing a hymn in the night, a shrouded figure lying face down on a chapel floor. Cosette is freezing. A man with a bell on his knee is working the melon beds, and when Valjean offers him money for shelter, the man greets him as “Father Madeleine.” It is old Fauchelevent, whom Madeleine once saved from under a cart and placed here as gardener. The house is the convent of the Petit-Picpus, and Fauchelevent hides them in his hut, asking no questions.

Hugo then tells the hunt from Javert’s side: transferred to Paris, he read of Valjean’s drowning, heard of a child taken from Montfermeil, tracked the “beggar who gives alms,” and delayed the arrest out of doubt until his quarry vanished. As chapter 118 closes, Valjean and Cosette are hidden inside a closed convent where no man may stay.

title: Inside the convent
text: Jean Valjean, the convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, and then gave himself up to save an innocent man. Escaping the galleys by letting the world believe him drowned, he took Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers and lived with her in Paris until Javert tracked him down. Fleeing by night, he climbed a wall with Cosette into the garden of the Petit-Picpus convent, where the gardener, old Fauchelevent, owes him his life and has hidden them.

Hugo then pauses for two long digressions: a guided tour of this strict convent of the Perpetual Adoration, with its veiled nuns, night offices and boarding-school of noble girls, and a “parenthesis” on convents in general, which he condemns as history but respects as an instrument of prayer.

To stay, Valjean must leave and come back in by the door. A nun, Mother Crucifixion, has died wishing to be buried secretly under the chapel altar, and the prioress has asked Fauchelevent to arrange it. Valjean has himself nailed into the empty official coffin and carried to the cemetery, where Fauchelevent means to dig him up. But the old gravedigger has died and his successor never drinks; earth falls on the lid and Valjean faints, until Fauchelevent steals the man’s card, sends him running home, and opens the coffin in time.

The prioress then receives Fauchelevent’s “brother,” Ultime Fauchelevent, as a second gardener, and admits Cosette as a pupil. Valjean never goes out, gardens beside his friend, sees Cosette an hour a day, and prays each evening outside the chapel; Javert watches the quarter for a month and then gives up. As chapter 146 closes, the years are passing behind the convent walls and Cosette is growing up.

title: Paris and its gamin
text: Jean Valjean, a convict whom the Bishop of Digne answered with mercy, became M. Madeleine, the good mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer, gave himself up to save an innocent man, escaped the galleys, and kept his word to the dead Fantine by taking her daughter, Cosette, from the cruel Thénardiers at Montfermeil. Hunted through Paris by Javert, he found refuge in the convent of the Petit-Picpus, where he passes as the gardener’s brother and Cosette is a pupil. Elsewhere, the reader knows that Thénardier robbed a wounded officer named Pontmercy on the night of Waterloo and that the officer believes he was saved.

Volume III begins with a long portrait of the Paris gamin, the ragged, cheeky, homeless street boy who knows every policeman and every execution, and through him of Paris itself, the city Hugo calls the sum of all history.

Then, eight or nine years after Valjean disappeared into the convent, he shows one such boy: Little Gavroche, eleven years old, merry and unloved, roaming the Boulevard du Temple. His family, the destitute Jondrettes, live in the Gorbeau house, next door to a poor young man known as M. Marius. As chapter 159 closes, Hugo has said nothing yet of what became of Valjean and Cosette.

title: Marius Pontmercy
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, took Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers in 1823 and vanished with her into the convent of the Petit-Picpus. Years have passed. In about 1831 a street boy, Little Gavroche, belongs to a wretched family called the Jondrettes who live in the Gorbeau house beside a poor young man, M. Marius. And on the night of Waterloo, Thénardier robbed a wounded officer, Pontmercy, who believes Thénardier saved his life.

Hugo now goes back to tell Marius’s story. M. Gillenormand is a loud, hale old royalist of over ninety, living in the Marais with his spinster daughter. His younger daughter married a soldier he despised and died, and he took their small son, Marius, from his father by threatening to disinherit the boy. The father is that very officer, Colonel Georges Pontmercy, made a baron by Napoleon at Waterloo and living on half-pay at Vernon, where he grows flowers and slips into church to watch his son from behind a pillar. Marius grows up a royalist, ashamed of his “brigand” father.

In 1827, at seventeen, Marius is sent to his dying father and arrives too late. He keeps a note in which the colonel leaves him his title and asks him to do all the good he can to a sergeant named Thénardier, who saved his life at Waterloo. The reader knows that “rescue” was a robbery; Marius does not. When an old churchwarden, M. Mabeuf, tells him how his father came secretly to mass for years just to see him, Marius is overwhelmed. He reads the history of the Empire, turns ardent Bonapartist, has cards printed as Baron Marius Pontmercy, and searches Montfermeil in vain for Thénardier, whose inn has failed.

His aunt sends her favourite, the lancer Théodule, to spy on his absences, and he finds Marius weeping at his father’s grave. Then the grandfather finds the colonel’s note and the cards. As chapter 175 closes, Marius has shouted “Down with the Bourbons!” and walked out with thirty francs, cut off from his family.

title: The Friends of the A.B.C.
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, disappeared years ago into a Paris convent with Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, whom he rescued from the Thénardiers. Around 1831 the street boy Gavroche belongs to the Jondrettes, a wretched family in the Gorbeau house, next door to a poor young man called Marius. Hugo has gone back to show how Marius came to be there. Raised by his royalist grandfather, M. Gillenormand, he discovered too late that his father, Colonel Pontmercy, had loved him in secret; he became a Bonapartist and quarrelled with the old man, and has left home with almost nothing. He also treasures his father’s wish that he help a sergeant named Thénardier who “saved” the colonel at Waterloo; the reader knows Thénardier was robbing him.

In the street Marius is hailed by Bossuet, who once answered for him at roll-call, and Courfeyrac takes him in. Through Courfeyrac he meets the Friends of the A.B.C., a small secret society of republican students who meet at the Café Musain: the stern, beautiful Enjolras, the thoughtful Combeferre, the poet Jean Prouvaire, the self-taught worker Feuilly, the brawler Bahorel, the unlucky Bossuet, the hypochondriac Joly, and Grantaire, a drunken sceptic who believes only in Enjolras.

Their irreverent talk shakes the beliefs Marius thought he had settled. When he makes a passionate speech for Napoleon, Combeferre answers “To be free,” and Enjolras tells him, “My mother is the Republic.” Unsettled, Marius stops going. As chapter 181 closes, he has sold his clothes and watch to pay his bill, returned the money his aunt sent, and left the hotel rather than run into debt.

title: Marius poor
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, disappeared years ago into a Paris convent with Cosette, the daughter of the dead Fantine, whom he took from the cruel Thénardiers in 1823. The story has moved on to about 1831 and to Marius Pontmercy. Raised by his royalist grandfather, M. Gillenormand, Marius learned too late that his father, Colonel Pontmercy, had loved him in secret; he became a fervent Bonapartist, quarrelled with the old man and left home. His father’s last wish was that he help a sergeant named Thénardier who “saved” him at Waterloo, though the reader knows Thénardier was robbing him. Through Courfeyrac, Marius has met the Friends of the A.B.C., Enjolras’s band of republican students, whose ideas have shaken his own.

Now Marius learns real poverty: days without bread, a coat worn only after dark so its green can pass for black. He becomes a lawyer but lives on hack work for a publisher, rents a fireless room in the Gorbeau house, and never runs into debt. He keeps returning his aunt’s money. Beside his father’s name he reveres Thénardier’s, and has searched for him in vain for years. His friends are Courfeyrac and old M. Mabeuf, the churchwarden who told him about his father, a gentle soul who loves only plants and old books and is sliding into poverty himself.

At twenty Marius is proud, solitary and given to dreaming; his political fever has cooled. Learning that his wretched neighbours, the Jondrettes, are about to be evicted, he secretly pays their rent. His grandfather, meanwhile, pines for him without taking a step, and the aunt’s attempt to replace him with her nephew Théodule ends with the old man calling the lancer a fool. As chapter 187 closes, the grandfather and grandson are each too proud to give way.

title: The girl at the Luxembourg
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, vanished years ago into a Paris convent with Cosette, the orphaned daughter of Fantine, whom he took from the Thénardiers. The story now follows Marius Pontmercy, about twenty in 1831: a poor young lawyer living in a bare room in the Gorbeau house, estranged from his royalist grandfather, M. Gillenormand, since he discovered and came to revere his dead father, Colonel Pontmercy. He reveres too the name of Thénardier, who his father believed saved him at Waterloo; the reader knows Thénardier robbed him. Marius has secretly paid the rent of his wretched neighbours, the Jondrettes.

For a year Marius has noticed, on a quiet walk in the Luxembourg Gardens, a white-haired man of about sixty and a plain, thin girl of thirteen or fourteen who sit on the same bench every day. Courfeyrac has nicknamed them Monsieur Leblanc and Mademoiselle Lanoire. After six months away, Marius comes back and finds the awkward child has become a beautiful young woman. One spring day their eyes meet, and he falls desperately in love.

For weeks he walks past in his one good coat, hides behind statues to be seen by her and not by her father, and lives on her glances, which she returns. He finds a handkerchief marked U. F. on their bench, decides her name is Ursule, and worships it. M. Leblanc seems to notice him, changes benches, and sometimes comes alone. Marius follows them home to the Rue de l’Ouest and questions the porter, and the next evening M. Leblanc stares hard at him at the gate. As chapter 196 closes, the pair have stopped coming to the Luxembourg and moved away without leaving an address, and Marius has lost her; he does not know who they are.

title: The trap in the Gorbeau house
text: Years ago Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, took Fantine’s little daughter, Cosette, from the Thénardiers at Montfermeil and vanished with her into a Paris convent. The story now follows Marius Pontmercy, a poor young lawyer estranged from his royalist grandfather, who reveres his dead father and the name of Thénardier, the sergeant his father believed had saved him at Waterloo. Marius fell in love with a girl he saw daily in the Luxembourg with a white-haired man he calls M. Leblanc, then lost them both. Hugo has also introduced Patron-Minette, the four-headed gang of Babet, Gueulemer, Claquesous and Montparnasse who rule the Paris underworld.

In February 1832 Marius finds a packet of begging letters dropped by two ragged girls, and the elder Jondrette daughter, from the hovel next door, comes begging with another in the same hand. Through a hole in the wall he watches the family stage their misery for a visiting philanthropist, and the visitors are M. Leblanc and the girl of the Luxembourg. Jondrette, passing himself off as a ruined actor, recognises the man from eight years back and plots to rob him when he returns that evening with money, helped by Patron-Minette. Marius runs to the police; a grim inspector named Javert gives him two pistols and tells him to fire a shot when the crime begins. Meanwhile the elder daughter has offered to find the girl’s address for him.

At six M. Leblanc returns to a room with a brazier and a red-hot chisel, and masked men close in. Jondrette drops his disguise: he is Thénardier, the innkeeper of Montfermeil, and he accuses his prisoner of being the man who carried off Fantine’s child, the Lark, on Christmas Eve 1823. So M. Leblanc is Jean Valjean, and the girl Marius loves is Cosette. Marius, hearing the name his father commanded him to honour, cannot bring himself to fire. The prisoner, bound, gives a false address, then frees a hand and burns his own arm with the chisel to show he cannot be made to speak. As Thénardier advances with a knife, Marius warns the gang with a scrap of paper, and Javert walks in and arrests them all, catching the younger girl, Azelma, but not her sister Éponine. When he turns to the victim, he has escaped through the window.

As chapter 222 closes, the next night Gavroche, the Thénardiers’ son, comes to visit his family and learns that his father is in La Force, his mother and sisters in other prisons; he says “Ah!” and goes off singing. Marius still does not know who M. Leblanc and his daughter are, or where they have gone.

title: Éponine
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, has been living in Paris with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, whom he took from the Thénardiers in 1823. Marius Pontmercy, a poor young lawyer who reveres his dead father, Colonel Pontmercy, fell in love with Cosette at the Luxembourg without knowing who she or her father, whom he calls M. Leblanc, were. In February 1832 Marius’s neighbour Jondrette, revealed as Thénardier, lured Valjean into a trap; Marius, unable to fire on the man his father told him to honour, warned the gang, Inspector Javert arrested them, and Valjean escaped through the window. Gavroche, the street boy, is Thénardier’s son.

Hugo opens Volume IV with history: the July Revolution of 1830, the reign of Louis Philippe, and the ferment of 1832, when secret societies are making cartridges in the faubourgs. Enjolras sends each of the Friends of the A.B.C. to sound out fighters across Paris; Grantaire, sent to the workmen of the Barrière du Maine, is found playing dominoes.

Marius has left the Gorbeau house to lodge with Courfeyrac, and every week sends five borrowed francs to Thénardier in La Force. He knows less than ever about the girl and drifts in daydreams in a lonely field the locals call the Lark’s meadow. Javert’s catch was incomplete: the victim escaped, Montparnasse got away, and Claquesous vanished on the way to prison. From La Force the gang sends out a note about a house in the Rue Plumet with a garden gate; Éponine, released, looks into it and sends back the signal for “nothing to be done.”

Éponine then turns up at old M. Mabeuf’s garden, waters it for him, and asks where Marius is. As chapter 232 closes, she has found him in the Lark’s meadow and offered to take him to the young lady’s house. Overjoyed, he makes her swear not to tell her father the address, and does not see how it hurts her; when he offers her five francs she lets the coin fall: “I don’t want your money.”

title: The house in the Rue Plumet
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, has raised Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, since taking her from the Thénardiers in 1823. Marius Pontmercy, a poor young lawyer, fell in love with her at the Luxembourg, not knowing who she or “M. Leblanc” were, and then lost them. In February 1832 Thénardier, living as Jondrette next door to Marius, trapped Valjean; Javert arrested the gang, Valjean escaped, and Marius still knows nothing. Now Éponine, Thénardier’s elder daughter, has found the girl’s address for Marius.

Hugo now tells the story from the other side. Since 1829 Valjean has lived as M. Fauchelevent in a hidden house in the Rue Plumet, with a secret passage to the Rue de Babylone and a wild, overgrown garden. When old Fauchelevent died, he left the convent so that Cosette would not take the veil before she had seen the world. He keeps two other lodgings, one in the Rue de l’Homme Armé, so he can vanish at the first alarm. Cosette has the pretty pavilion; he lives in a bare lodge, serves in the National Guard, and gives alms with her. She adores him. She does not know her mother’s name, and when she asks, he is silent.

At fifteen Cosette discovers she is beautiful. The Luxembourg is retold from her side: Marius’s glances troubled her as much as hers did him, and she loved him without a word, without even knowing his name. Valjean sensed the young man, hated him, and after Marius followed them home he left the Luxembourg for good. Father and daughter now suffer side by side in silence.

As chapter 240 closes, the two have watched a chain-gang pass at dawn on its way to the galleys, collared men in carts, singing and cursing. Valjean was petrified; Cosette asks him what the galleys are like.

title: A letter under a stone
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent in a secluded house in the Rue Plumet with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, whom he took from the Thénardiers as a child. Marius Pontmercy, a poor young lawyer, fell in love with Cosette at the Luxembourg, and she with him, without a word exchanged; Valjean took her away from the gardens. In February 1832 Thénardier lured Valjean into a trap in the Gorbeau house; Javert arrested the gang and Valjean escaped, while Marius, Thénardier’s neighbour, still does not know who “M. Leblanc” and his daughter are. Éponine, Thénardier’s elder daughter, has found their address for Marius.

Valjean came home from the Jondrette den with his arm burned; for a month Cosette nursed him, the old closeness returned, and he blessed the wound. Meanwhile Gavroche, hungry, watches an elderly passer-by overpower the young thug Montparnasse, lecture him on the hard labour of crime, and give him his purse; Gavroche picks it from Montparnasse’s pocket and throws it over the hedge to the penniless M. Mabeuf.

Cosette’s sadness fades, and she starts watching for a handsome lancer who rides past the gate, Théodule Gillenormand. While Valjean is away on one of his short, unexplained trips, she hears steps in the garden and sees a man’s shadow. Then she finds an envelope under a stone on her bench: a notebook of unsigned thoughts on love, and she knows at once who wrote it. The lancer is forgotten.

As chapter 248 closes, Marius has come to her in the garden at dusk while her father is out. He tells her how he searched for her; she faints in his arms; they kiss and talk for hours, and only at the very end tell each other their names: Marius, Cosette.

title: Little Gavroche
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent in the Rue Plumet with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, whom he rescued from the Thénardiers. Marius Pontmercy, the poor young lawyer who fell in love with her at the Luxembourg, has found her garden, and in the spring of 1832 the two have at last met and exchanged names. Valjean knows nothing of it. Thénardier, who trapped Valjean in the Gorbeau house in February, is in La Force with his gang; Valjean escaped, and Marius still does not know who his beloved’s father is.

Hugo now explains that the Thénardiers had two more sons after 1823 and handed them, for money, to a woman called Magnon, to stand in for her own dead boys, whose upkeep M. Gillenormand had agreed to pay. After the Jondrette arrests, the little boys are locked out of Magnon’s house and wander the streets, lost.

On a freezing, stormy night Gavroche takes in two small lost boys, not knowing they are his brothers. He buys them bread with his last sou and beds them down in his home, the giant plaster elephant on the Place de la Bastille. Before dawn Montparnasse calls him out to help. That night Brujon, Gueulemer and Thénardier have broken out of La Force, but Thénardier is stranded on top of a ruined wall with a rope too short. Gavroche climbs a flue with the rope in his teeth and brings him down, recognising his own father and shrugging that it makes no difference.
As chapter 251 closes, Thénardier, free, has barely glanced at the boy and is already talking with the gang about the job in the Rue Plumet; Gavroche goes back to his two little lodgers.

title: Enchantments and desolations
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent in a hidden house in the Rue Plumet with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, whom he rescued as a child from the Thénardiers. Marius Pontmercy, a poor young lawyer estranged from his royalist grandfather, fell in love with her at the Luxembourg and has found her garden. Thénardier, who once trapped Valjean in the Gorbeau house, has broken out of La Force with his son Gavroche’s help, and the gang has its eye on the Rue Plumet. After a long digression on thieves’ slang, Hugo returns to the lovers.

Every evening in May 1832 Marius slips through a loose bar in the gate and spends hours with Cosette in the garden. Their love is innocent: hands held, nonsense talked, the discovery that her real name is Euphrasie. Neither asks where it is leading, and Marius never mentions the Gorbeau ambush or her father’s strange flight. Éponine stops him once in the street and leaves without finding words.

On the night of 3 June Éponine is sitting by the gate when six men come to rob the house: her father, Claquesous, Gueulemer, Babet, Brujon and Montparnasse. She faces them down alone, threatening to scream for the police, and they withdraw. That same evening Cosette tells Marius, in tears, that her father means to take her away within the week, perhaps to England. Marius, penniless, swears he would die if she went, scratches his address, 16 Rue de la Verrerie, on the garden wall, and says he is going to try something.

He goes to his grandfather for the first time in four years to ask permission to marry Mademoiselle Fauchelevent. The old man, who has been pining for him, meets him gruffly, softens, then ruins everything by advising him to make the girl his mistress. As chapter 262 closes, Marius has left with a farewell, and M. Gillenormand has collapsed calling his name.

title: The eve of the rising
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent in the Rue Plumet with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, whom he rescued as a child from the Thénardiers. All through May 1832 Marius Pontmercy, the poor young lawyer who fell in love with her at the Luxembourg, has met her secretly in the garden; Valjean knows nothing of it. On the night of 3 June Thénardier’s elder daughter, Éponine, who loves Marius, turned her father’s gang away from the house. That evening Cosette told Marius that her father was taking her away, perhaps to England, and Marius, after scratching his address on the garden wall, went to ask his grandfather’s consent to marry her and left in despair.

On 4 June Valjean sits alone on the Champ-de-Mars, resolved to leave France within the week: he has seen Thénardier prowling the boulevards, and Paris is restless with police. That morning he found an unknown address freshly scratched on his garden wall. Now a folded paper drops on his knees, reading “Move away from your house,” and a slight figure in a grey blouse and velvet trousers vanishes over the parapet.
Old M. Mabeuf, ruined, has sold his books one by one for bread, the last of them on 4 June. The next afternoon, hearing that there is fighting in Paris, he puts on his hat and walks out.

Marius wanders the streets for a day and a night, pockets the two loaded pistols Javert once gave him, and at nine on 5 June goes to the Rue Plumet. The shutters are closed, the garden is empty, and no one answers when he calls. Cosette is gone and he does not know where. As chapter 265 closes, he has resolved to die, and a voice from the street has called through the trees that his friends are waiting for him at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.

title: The 5th of June, 1832
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, and has resolved to leave France after seeing Thénardier prowl near their house and receiving an anonymous warning to move. Marius Pontmercy, who has loved Cosette in secret all spring, has found her house in the Rue Plumet shut and empty. Despairing, carrying Javert’s two pistols, he has been called by a voice in the dark to join his friends at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.

Hugo first sets out what a revolt is, and then tells how the rising began. On 5 June 1832 the funeral of General Lamarque, a popular hero, crosses Paris amid an armed, excited crowd; at the Austerlitz bridge shots are fired, dragoons charge, and within an hour barricades are rising across a third of the city.

Gavroche borrows an old pistol with no trigger and marches off to the war singing, smashing on his way the window of the barber who once turned his two little lodgers away; the two lost boys never came back to the elephant. He joins the armed band of Enjolras, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Feuilly, Bahorel and Jean Prouvaire, and with them, unarmed and hatless, walks old M. Mabeuf, who has told Courfeyrac that bringing down the government “is good.”

As chapter 276 closes, a tall, grey-haired stranger of bold bearing has quietly joined the column, and at Courfeyrac’s lodging a pale young workman who has been waiting an hour to ask for Marius has decided to come along. The crowd is moving toward the Rue Saint-Denis.

title: The barricade at Corinthe
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, and is preparing to leave France. Marius Pontmercy, who loves Cosette, found her house empty on the evening of 5 June 1832, as a riot broke out across Paris after General Lamarque’s funeral; despairing, he has been called by a voice to join his friends at the barricade. Enjolras and the Friends of the A.B.C. are marching with Gavroche, old M. Mabeuf, a tall stranger who joined on the way, and a young workman asking for Marius.

Bossuet, Joly and Grantaire are drinking at Corinthe, the old wine-shop in the Rue de la Chanvrerie, when the column passes, and Bossuet calls out that this is the place for a barricade. In minutes the street is closed with paving-stones, casks and an overturned omnibus, with a smaller barricade around the corner. Grantaire, roaring drunk, is sent off the barricade by Enjolras, swears “You will see,” and falls asleep at a table. Bullets are cast from the widow Hucheloup’s pewter, cartridges handed out, and fifty men wait in the twilight.

Enjolras sends Gavroche to scout, but the boy first points out the tall stranger as a police spy. He is Javert. Searched and found to carry an inspector’s card, he is tied to a post in the taproom and told he would be shot ten minutes before the barricade falls. Then a drunken recruit, Le Cabuc, shoots an old porter who refuses to let him into a house; Enjolras makes him kneel and executes him, saying a revolution must have its discipline and that he has judged himself too. Police tradition, Hugo adds, says Le Cabuc was Claquesous of Patron-Minette.
As chapter 284 closes, night has fallen on the barricade, the young workman who asked for Marius has reappeared on it, and Marius himself has not yet come.

title: Éponine’s letter
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, lives as M. Fauchelevent with Cosette, Fantine’s daughter, and is preparing to leave France. Marius Pontmercy, who loves Cosette, found her house empty on 5 June 1832, the day a rising broke out in Paris, and was called by a voice to the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie, where Enjolras and the Friends of the A.B.C. hold the wine-shop Corinthe. Javert, unmasked there as a police spy, is bound in the taproom under sentence of death.

Marius crosses darkened Paris toward the barricade and hesitates at its edge, thinking of his soldier father, before deciding that civil war is not a betrayal of him. At ten the troops attack and shoot down the flag. Old M. Mabeuf climbs the barricade with it, cries “Long live the Republic!” and is killed. Bahorel falls; Gavroche is about to be bayoneted when Marius arrives and shoots two guardsmen. A young workman puts a hand over a musket aimed at Marius and falls. Marius drives the troops back by threatening to blow up the barricade with a barrel of powder, and Enjolras makes him a chief. Jean Prouvaire, taken prisoner, is shot by the troops.

At the small barricade Marius hears his name: the dying young workman is Éponine in men’s clothes. She led him here so they could die together; the singing street boy, she tells him, is her brother. She gives him a letter she had kept from him, asks for a kiss on her brow when she is dead, and dies. Hugo explains that she was also the figure who warned Valjean to move. The letter is from Cosette: her father took her on 4 June to 7 Rue de l’Homme Armé, and they leave for England in a week.

As chapter 294 closes, Marius, sure he is going to die, has written a farewell to Cosette and a note asking that his body be taken to his grandfather, and sent Gavroche across Paris with the letter, to get the boy out of the fight. Gavroche means to be back before the barricade falls.

title: The Rue de l’Homme Armé
text: On 5 June 1832 a rising broke out in Paris. At the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie, Enjolras and the Friends of the A.B.C. hold out with Marius Pontmercy, who came there in despair after losing Cosette. Old M. Mabeuf and Jean Prouvaire have been killed, and Éponine, disguised as a workman, died in Marius’s arms after taking a bullet meant for him. She gave him Cosette’s letter with her new address in the Rue de l’Homme Armé, and Marius has sent Gavroche there with his farewell. Javert, unmasked as a spy, is bound in the wine-shop.

The narrator turns back to Jean Valjean. On the evening of 4 June he moved Cosette and their servant, Toussaint, to his spare lodging in the Rue de l’Homme Armé, carrying only his “inseparable” little valise, and by the next evening he felt at peace again. Then in a mirror he read the reversed imprint of Cosette’s note to Marius on her blotter. His world went dark; he guessed the man was the prowler of the Luxembourg and found hatred in his heart.

Sitting on the post by his door at night, he meets Gavroche searching for number 7, claims to be the person the letter is for, and takes it. Upstairs he reads “I die,” and feels a frightful joy: the man who stands between him and Cosette is going to his death of his own accord. Then he grows gloomy, and an hour later goes out, armed and in his National Guard uniform, toward the markets. Cosette, asleep, knows nothing.
As chapter 298 closes, Gavroche is running back toward the barricade with a stolen handcart, having escaped a volley from a National Guard post, worried only that he may be late.

title: The fall of the barricade
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, has raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own and was about to take her to England when he learned that she loves Marius Pontmercy. On the night of 5 June 1832 he intercepted Marius’s farewell letter, written at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie, where Enjolras and the Friends of the A.B.C. are holding out and where Mabeuf, Prouvaire and Éponine have died. Then he went out in his National Guard uniform. Javert, unmasked as a spy, is bound in the wine-shop.

By dawn thirty-seven men remain. Enjolras tells them the truth: Paris is not rising and they are alone. The fathers among them are sent away in captured uniforms, and when one uniform is short, a fifth falls on the pile: Valjean has come in. Marius knows him as M. Fauchelevent; the bound Javert recognises him and remarks only that it is perfectly simple. Valjean fights without killing, shooting down a mattress to stop the cannon and knocking helmets off watchers on the roofs. Gavroche, back from his errand, slips out to gather cartridges from the dead and is shot, still singing. Far away in the Luxembourg, his two little brothers share a stale brioche fished from the swans’ basin.

When Enjolras orders that the last man to leave the taproom shall shoot the spy, Valjean asks for the task. Out of sight, he cuts Javert’s bonds, tells him he lives at 7 Rue de l’Homme Armé under the name Fauchelevent, lets him go, and fires into the air. Marius, who has just recognised Javert, hears the shot and believes him dead.

In the final assault Bossuet, Feuilly, Courfeyrac and Combeferre are killed. Enjolras holds the door alone, then faces a firing squad upstairs, and Grantaire, waking from his stupor, asks to die with him; they fall together. Marius was struck down outside and felt a hand seize him. As chapter 322 closes, that hand is Valjean’s: trapped with the unconscious Marius, he has found an iron grating under the paving-stones and carried him down into the sewers of Paris.

title: Through the sewer
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, has raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own; on 5 June 1832 he discovered that she loves Marius Pontmercy, who had gone to die at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie. Valjean went there himself. He freed Javert, who had been captured as a spy, letting Marius believe he had shot him. Then the barricade fell, with Enjolras, Gavroche and all their friends dead, and Valjean carried the wounded, unconscious Marius down through a grating into the sewers.

Hugo first tours the sewer of Paris, its history and its waste, and the brave engineer Bruneseau who mapped it. Then Valjean, bent double under Marius, gropes through the dark, hides from a police patrol, reads in Marius’s pocket the address of his grandfather, M. Gillenormand, and nearly drowns in a sinkhole of mud, holding Marius above it. He reaches an outlet on the Seine, but it is locked.

There Thénardier finds him. Not recognising the mud-covered Valjean, he takes him for a murderer getting rid of a body, takes his money, secretly tears a strip from Marius’s coat, and unlocks the grating, using Valjean as a decoy for the man who has been tailing him outside. That man is Javert. Valjean gives his name and surrenders, asking only to carry Marius home first; Javert brings them by cab to the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, then agrees to let Valjean stop at his own door. Valjean goes upstairs meaning to warn Cosette and settle his affairs before surrendering; when he looks out of the landing window, the street is empty and Javert has gone.
As chapter 340 closes, Marius lies at his grandfather’s gravely wounded. The old man, thinking him dead, rages and weeps, and then Marius opens his eyes.

title: Grandson and grandfather
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, has raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own and lives with her as M. Fauchelevent. On 6 June 1832, when the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie fell with Enjolras, Gavroche and their friends, he carried Marius Pontmercy, the young man Cosette loves, through the sewers. Thénardier let them out; Javert, waiting at the outlet, arrested Valjean, let him take Marius home to his grandfather, M. Gillenormand, and then let him go. At the barricade Valjean had already spared Javert’s life.

Unable to arrest the man who spared him or to let him go, Javert writes a few notes on police service and throws himself into the Seine. Near Montfermeil the road-mender Boulatruelle follows a man into the forest and finds only an empty hole.

For months Marius hovers between life and death, visited daily by a white-haired gentleman who leaves lint. His grandfather is transformed by joy, and when Marius asks to marry, he agrees at once; he has already found Cosette. She comes with “M. Fauchelevent,” who is Jean Valjean, and he announces that she has six hundred thousand francs. The narrator explains that this is the money he earned as M. Madeleine and buried with the Bishop’s candlesticks in the forest of Montfermeil; he was the man Boulatruelle saw, and he has read in the papers that Javert drowned. He gives Cosette a legal name, Euphrasie Fauchelevent, the old man showers her with heirlooms, and the wedding is set for February.

Marius, his memory clouded, begins to think he imagined M. Fauchelevent at the barricade. He searches for two men: Thénardier, whose wife has died in prison and who has been condemned to death in his absence and has vanished, and the unknown man who carried him through the sewer, of whom he has only a cabman’s story and a torn, bloodstained coat. As chapter 349 closes, Marius has sworn he would give Cosette’s whole fortune to find his rescuer, and Valjean has said nothing.

title: The wedding
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own under the name of Fauchelevent. In June 1832 he carried the wounded Marius Pontmercy, the young man Cosette loves, out of the fallen barricade and through the sewers to his grandfather’s house; Javert, who had arrested him at the outlet, let him go and then drowned himself in the Seine. Marius, recovered and reconciled with M. Gillenormand, is to marry Cosette, who brings a dowry of six hundred thousand francs, the money Valjean earned as M. Madeleine. Marius does not know who saved him, and Valjean has not told him.

On 16 February 1833, Shrove Tuesday, Marius and Cosette are married. The night before, Valjean handed over the fortune; he wears his arm in a sling, pleading a crushed thumb, so that he need not sign anything, and the grandfather gives the bride away. On the way to the church the carriages stop beside a cart of carnival maskers, and an old “Spaniard” among them recognises the man with his arm in a sling and orders his companion, Azelma, to find out where the wedding is going.

At the banquet Valjean’s chair stands empty; he has slipped away, pleading his hand. He walks home alone to the Rue de l’Homme Armé, takes off the sling, opens his little valise and lays out the mourning clothes Cosette wore as a child when he led her out of Montfermeil, and weeps over them.

As chapter 353 closes, he has spent the whole night wrestling with his conscience for what he feels is the last time: whether to keep his place beside Cosette in her new family, with his past hidden, or to tell the truth and let her go. Dawn finds him still prostrate over her little clothes, and the narrator has not said what he has decided.

title: Valjean’s confession
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own under the name of Fauchelevent. In June 1832 he carried the wounded Marius Pontmercy out of the fallen barricade and through the sewers to his grandfather’s house; Javert let him go and then drowned himself in the Seine. Marius does not know who saved him. On 16 February 1833 Marius married Cosette, with a dowry of six hundred thousand francs from Valjean, who slipped away from the wedding feast and spent the night in torment over what to do.

The next morning he asks to see Marius alone. He unwraps his bandage to show an uninjured thumb and tells him the truth: he is an ex-convict named Jean Valjean, nineteen years in the galleys and still a fugitive, and no relation of Cosette’s. Marius promises to keep the secret and coldly agrees that it would be better if Valjean stopped seeing her, then relents when Valjean begs, and tells him to come every evening.

Alone, Marius turns it over. The returned fortune and the voluntary confession speak for an awakened conscience, yet he concludes that Valjean fled the Gorbeau trap because he was a fugitive, and went to the barricade to take revenge on Javert, whose execution Marius thinks he heard. He recoils from the convict, and realises he did not dare to ask the questions that mattered. As chapter 355 closes, Cosette knows nothing; the reader knows that Valjean freed Javert, and Marius does not.

title: Monsieur Jean
text: Jean Valjean, the convict redeemed by the Bishop of Digne’s mercy, raised Fantine’s daughter, Cosette, as his own and gave her a fortune when she married Marius Pontmercy in February 1833. Marius does not know that Valjean carried him out of the barricade and through the sewers in June 1832, or that Javert drowned himself after letting Valjean go. The morning after the wedding, Valjean told Marius he was an ex-convict and no relation of Cosette’s. Marius kept the secret but has come to believe Valjean killed Javert, and allowed him only evening visits.

Valjean asks to be received in a damp ground-floor room. He refuses Cosette’s kisses, asks her to call him “Monsieur Jean” and addresses her as “Madame”; she is hurt and puzzled, then, soothed by Marius, accepts it, and the household decides he is an eccentric. Evening after evening he loosens her from himself, and when she once slips and calls him “father,” he corrects her and hides his tears.

One evening the couple go off to revisit their old garden in the Rue Plumet and he waits in vain. Then the fire in the lower room is left unlit and the armchairs disappear, and he understands he is being shown the door. He sends word that he is busy and about to travel, and stops coming.

As chapter 359 closes, it is the summer of 1833. Every evening an old man in black walks from the Rue de l’Homme Armé toward the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, peers round the corner, weeps, and turns back; each day the walk is shorter, until he no longer gets past the Blancs-Manteaux.
